AUD-001.e: The auditor adjusts detection risk (nature, timing, extent of substantive procedures) to the assessed risk of material misstatement.
o: Risk of material misstatement (inherent × control risk) and detection risk
FX risk and interest rate risk
AUD-001.x:
Basis: VSA 200 para 13, A32–A44; VSA 315.
Analysis: Audit risk = risk of material misstatement (RMM) × detection risk. RMM comprises inherent and control risk – existing independently of the audit, merely assessed by the auditor. Detection risk is what the auditor controls via the nature, timing and extent of substantive procedures: higher RMM → lower acceptable detection risk → more work.
Distractors: B, C and D are the entity's business/financial risks, not audit-risk components.

AUD-002.q: Audit risk model: acceptable audit risk 5%; inherent risk 80%; control risk 50%. What is the maximum acceptable detection risk (%)?
AUD-002.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (audit risk model).
Working: DR = AR / (IR × CR) = 5% / (0.8 × 0.5) = 5% / 0.4 = 12.5%.
Analysis: Maximum acceptable detection risk is 12.5% → substantive procedures must be designed so the chance of missing a material misstatement doesn't exceed it.
Check: 0.8 × 0.5 × 0.125 = 0.05 ✓.
Note: The multiplicative model is conceptual; VSA calls for judgement, not mandatory quantification.

AUD-003.q: A manufacturer has stable profit before tax of VND 40 billion; the auditor sets overall materiality at 5% of PBT. What is overall materiality (VND billion)?
AUD-003.e: 40 × 5% = 2 billion VND. The exact percentage is professional judgement per firm policy.
AUD-003.x:
Basis: VSA 320 para 10, A3–A8.
Working: Overall materiality = 40 × 5% = VND 2 billion.
Analysis: PBT suits a manufacturer with stable profits because users focus on profit. 5% is common practice (VSA 320 A7 gives 5% of PBT from continuing operations as an example); the exact rate is judgement under firm policy.
Check: 2 / 40 = 5% ✓.

AUD-004.q: A manufacturer has stable profit before tax of VND 40 billion; the auditor sets overall materiality at 5% of PBT, performance materiality at 75% and the clearly trivial threshold at 5% of overall materiality. What is the clearly trivial threshold (VND million)?
AUD-004.e: Performance materiality = 1.5 billion; trivial threshold = 2 billion × 5% = 100 million VND.
AUD-004.x:
Basis: VSA 320 para 11 (performance materiality); VSA 450 para 5, A2 (clearly trivial threshold).
Working: Overall = 40 × 5% = 2 billion; performance = 2 × 75% = 1.5 billion; trivial threshold = 2 billion × 5% = VND 100 million.
Analysis: Misstatements below 100 million needn't be accumulated in the unadjusted schedule (unless qualitatively significant). Performance materiality sits below overall materiality to reduce the chance that uncorrected plus undetected misstatements exceed it.

AUD-005.q: A loss-making tech start-up with rapid revenue growth is valued by investors on revenue. The most suitable materiality benchmark:
AUD-005.e: When profit is negative/volatile, pick a stable benchmark that users focus on.
AUD-005.x:
Basis: VSA 320 paras A3–A6 (choosing a materiality benchmark).
Analysis: A loss-making start-up has negative/volatile profit → PBT isn't a stable, suitable benchmark. Investors value it on revenue → revenue (or total expenses) is what users care about most and is more stable.
Distractors: B – a negative profit can't serve as a base; C – equity suits investment funds and asset-holding entities; D – prior-year figures don't reflect current scale.

AUD-006.q: Under VSA 315, what must the auditor understand about the entity?
AUD-006.e: The first six are required areas under VSA 315; individual salaries are not.
o: Nature of the entity: operations, ownership, governance, investments, financing
Objectives, strategies and related business risks
Measurement and review of financial performance
Internal control relevant to the audit
AUD-006.x:
Basis: VSA 315 para 11 (understanding the entity and its environment).
Analysis: The auditor must understand: (A) industry, regulatory and external factors; (B) the entity's nature – operations, ownership, governance, investments, financing; (C) accounting policies and their appropriateness; (D) objectives, strategies and business risks that may cause misstatement; (E) performance measurement (which creates pressure); (F) relevant internal control (para 12).
Distractors: (G) Each accountant's salary isn't required.
Note: ISA 315 (Revised 2019) restructures these; the question follows the current VSA 315.

AUD-007.q: Under VSA 240, the auditor presumes a fraud risk in revenue recognition unless rebutted, with reasons documented.
AUD-007.e: True. It is a rebuttable presumption.
AUD-007.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 26, 47.
Analysis: True. The auditor must presume fraud risk in revenue recognition and evaluate which revenue types, transactions or assertions give rise to it. The presumption is rebuttable – e.g., simple rental income under one lease – but the reasons must be documented (para 47).

AUD-008.q: The risk of management override of controls can be rebutted if the entity's internal control is strong.
AUD-008.e: False. It exists in all entities and is always a significant risk; journal entry, estimate and unusual-transaction procedures are required.
AUD-008.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 31–33.
Analysis: False. Management override is present in every entity; it varies in degree but is always a fraud risk and a significant risk – not rebuttable even with good IC (those who set the controls can bypass them). Mandatory procedures: test journal entries and adjustments (AUD-050), review estimates for bias (AUD-069), evaluate the business rationale of unusual transactions.

AUD-009.q: A property developer's loan covenant requires debt/EBITDA ≤ 4x; this year it is 3.95x. The auditor should:
AUD-009.e: Being near a covenant threshold creates an incentive to manage earnings.
o: Treat it as pressure increasing fraudulent reporting risk; expand procedures on revenue, capitalised interest and estimates
Ignore it since there's no breach
AUD-009.x:
Basis: VSA 240 (appendix 1 – pressure factors); VSA 315.
Analysis: Net debt/EBITDA of 3.95 against a 4.0 covenant → strong pressure to lift EBITDA or understate debt to avoid a breach (acceleration). Expand work on revenue (early or fictitious), capitalised interest (lower expense, higher EBITDA), estimates (provisions, property inventory values) and debt classification.
Distractors: B – no breach yet doesn't mean no risk; C is insufficient; D isn't the auditor's role.

AUD-010.q: Match each assertion with a typical risk:
AUD-010.e: Risks are assessed at assertion level to design suitable procedures.
p: Next year's revenue booked this year
Recording assets that belong to others
AUD-010.x:
Basis: VSA 315 para A111 (assertions).
Analysis: Occurrence – recorded transactions happened → fictitious revenue risk. Completeness – all transactions recorded → omitted payables and expenses. Valuation – appropriate amounts → no write-down for obsolete stock. Cut-off – right period → next year's revenue booked this year. Rights and obligations – the entity holds rights to assets → recording others' assets; pledged assets must be disclosed.

AUD-011.q: Risk assessment procedures under VSA 315 include:
AUD-011.e: Risk assessment procedures alone do not give sufficient evidence for the opinion.
o: Inquiry, analytical procedures, observation and inspection
AUD-011.x:
Basis: VSA 315 para 6.
Analysis: Risk assessment procedures: inquiries of management and others; analytical procedures; observation and inspection. Purpose: understand the entity to identify and assess RMM at the FS and assertion levels.
Distractors: B, C and D – confirmations, tests of details and counts are further procedures (VSA 330), not the sole risk assessment procedures.
Note: Risk assessment procedures alone don't provide sufficient evidence for the audit opinion.

AUD-012.q: Select ALL features that often make a risk 'significant':
AUD-012.e: Routine automated transactions usually carry lower risk.
o: Unusual transactions outside the normal course
AUD-012.x:
Basis: VSA 315 paras 27–28 (significant risks).
Analysis: Features typically creating significant risk: (A) fraud; (B) unusual transactions outside the normal course of business; (C) estimates with high uncertainty and judgement; (D) complex related-party transactions (VSA 550).
Distractors: (E) Routine, automated, low-judgement transactions are usually lower risk and better controlled.

AUD-013.q: For a significant risk, if the auditor performs only substantive procedures, they must include tests of details, not just substantive analytics.
AUD-013.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 21.
Analysis: True. For a significant risk, if the approach is substantive only, it must include tests of details – substantive analytics alone aren't enough, because significant risks (often fraud or unusual transactions) don't follow stable data relationships.

AUD-014.q: The engagement team discussion under VSA 240 and VSA 315 aims to:
AUD-014.e: Discuss with professional scepticism, setting aside beliefs about management integrity.
o: Discuss susceptibility of the FS to material misstatement, including fraud, and how fraud might occur
AUD-014.x:
Basis: VSA 240 para 15; VSA 315 para 10.
Analysis: The team discussion shares knowledge of the entity and considers how the FS could be materially misstated, especially through fraud – where and how fraud might occur and be concealed by management – and agrees responses. It is conducted with professional scepticism, setting aside beliefs about management's integrity.
Distractors: B, C and D are administrative.

AUD-015.q: Preliminary analytics: last year's inventory turnover was 6x; this year COGS is VND 120 billion and average inventory 30 billion. What is this year's turnover (times)?
AUD-015.e: 120/30 = 4x (down from 6) → risk of slow-moving stock, valuation and fictitious inventory.
AUD-015.x:
Basis: VSA 315 para 6b; VSA 520.
Working: Inventory turnover = COGS / average inventory = 120 / 30 = 4 times (prior year 6).
Analysis: Days in inventory rise from about 61 (365/6) to about 91 (365/4) → risk of slow-moving or obsolete stock not written down (valuation), fictitious inventory (existence), or COGS cut-off errors.
Check: 30 × 4 = 120 ✓.

AUD-016.q: The entity switched ERP in September. The key audit risk:
AUD-016.e: Test migration balance reconciliations and controls of both old and new systems.
o: Completeness and accuracy of migrated data and controls during parallel run; two control environments in the year
None since the new ERP is better
AUD-016.x:
Basis: VSA 315 paras A89–A95 (IT and system change).
Analysis: A mid-year ERP switch creates risks: balances and master data migrated incompletely or inaccurately; duplicates or omissions during parallel running; two different control environments in one year (Jan–Sep old, Oct–Dec new). Procedures: reconcile migrated balances, test conversion controls, evaluate controls in both systems.
Distractors: B – a new system isn't automatically better; C and D aren't the core risk.

AUD-017.q: Before accepting a new audit client, the incoming auditor should:
AUD-017.e: This helps assess management integrity and engagement risk.
o: Contact the predecessor auditor (with client consent) about reasons for change and disagreements
AUD-017.x:
Basis: Code of ethics (changes in appointment); VSA 220 para 12; VSA 300 para 13; VSA 510.
Analysis: Before accepting, the incoming auditor should (with client permission) contact the predecessor about reasons for the change, disagreements with management on accounting or auditing, fraud indications and scope limits → assessing management integrity and engagement risk. A client refusing permission is a red flag.
Distractors: B, C and D don't assess acceptance risk.

AUD-018.q: The auditor performs tests of controls when:
AUD-018.e: In high-volume automated processing, substantive testing alone may be insufficient.
o: They plan to rely on controls to reduce substantive testing, or substantive procedures alone can't provide sufficient evidence
When there's no time for substantive work
AUD-018.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 8.
Analysis: Tests of controls are required when: (a) the risk assessment expects controls to operate effectively (planning to rely on them to cut substantive work); or (b) substantive procedures alone can't give sufficient evidence (e.g., high-volume automated processing with no paper trail).
Distractors: B – not required for every control; C and D aren't standards-based reasons.

AUD-019.q: Inquiry alone is not sufficient to test the operating effectiveness of controls.
AUD-019.e: True. It must be combined with inspection, observation or re-performance.
AUD-019.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 10a.
Analysis: True. Inquiry alone isn't enough to test operating effectiveness – what the performer says doesn't prove the control actually operated consistently over the period. Combine it with inspection, observation or re-performance (AUD-026).

AUD-020.q: The auditor wants to rely on control evidence from prior years. Under VSA 330, the condition is:
AUD-020.e: Controls mitigating significant risks must be tested in the current period.
o: Confirm the controls haven't changed and retest at least once every 3 years; controls over significant risks must be tested in the current year
Prior-year evidence may never be used
AUD-020.x:
Basis: VSA 330 paras 13–15.
Analysis: Using prior-audit control evidence requires: (1) evidence on whether the control changed since last tested (inquiry plus observation/inspection); if changed, retest this year; if not, retest at least once every 3 years. (2) Controls over significant risks must be tested in the current period.
Distractors: B, C and D misstate the rule.

AUD-021.q: Attribute sampling: sample of 60, 1 deviation; the table gives an upper deviation limit of 7.8% at 5% risk. The tolerable deviation rate is 5%. What is the gap between the upper limit and tolerable rate (percentage points)?
AUD-021.e: 7.8 − 5 = 2.8 > 0 → cannot conclude the control is effective at the planned confidence; raise assessed control risk.
AUD-021.x:
Basis: VSA 530 para 14, A21–A23.
Working: Difference = upper deviation limit − tolerable rate = 7.8% − 5% = 2.8 points.
Analysis: The upper limit (7.8%) exceeds the tolerable rate (5%) → at the planned confidence the control can't be concluded effective as expected → raise assessed control risk, extend substantive work or test compensating controls.
Note: The sample rate is only 1/60 ≈ 1.7%, but the conclusion rests on the upper limit, not the sample rate.

AUD-022.q: The auditor finds one deviation in a sample testing payment approvals. The correct next step:
AUD-022.e: Deviations must not be replaced to 'improve' results.
o: Understand the cause, judge whether isolated or systemic; consider extending the sample or compensating controls, and the effect on substantive work
Replace the faulty item with another
Ignore it since it's one item
AUD-022.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 17; VSA 530 paras 12–13.
Analysis: On finding a deviation: understand cause and nature (isolated or systemic, intentional?); evaluate the impact – extend the sample, test compensating controls, or don't rely and expand substantive work.
Distractors: B – replacing the failed item distorts results and breaches sampling principles; C – one deviation may signal a systemic issue; D contradicts the evidence.

AUD-023.q: Select ALL factors that INCREASE the sample size for tests of controls:
AUD-023.e: Large population size has little effect; very small populations can reduce sample size.
o: A much smaller population (a few dozen items)
AUD-023.x:
Basis: VSA 530 appendix 2 (factors affecting control-test sample size).
Analysis: Sample size increases with: (A) greater reliance on the control (stronger evidence needed); (B) a lower tolerable deviation rate; (C) a higher expected deviation rate; (D) higher desired confidence.
Distractors: (E) Population size has little effect for large populations; a very small one usually reduces size (or calls for testing all), not increases it.

AUD-024.q: The automated control 'ERP blocks duplicate invoice number and vendor' sits within effective ITGCs. A suitable test:
AUD-024.e: Automated controls operate consistently if the logic doesn't change.
o: Inspect configuration and attempt one duplicate (test of one), plus confirm effective change-management ITGCs all year
AUD-024.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para A29 (automated controls); VSA 315.
Analysis: An automated control operates consistently if logic doesn't change. Procedure: inspect the configuration (blocking duplicate invoice number + supplier) and run one duplicate (test of one), plus evidence that change-management and access ITGC were effective all year so the logic wasn't altered (ICA-040, ICA-063).
Distractors: B – a sample of 60 is the manual-control approach, inefficient here; C – inquiry isn't enough; D – it must be tested if relied on.

AUD-025.q: If controls are ineffective, the auditor can still give an unmodified opinion on the FS after extending substantive testing and obtaining sufficient appropriate evidence.
AUD-025.e: True. The FS opinion is not an opinion on internal control; significant deficiencies are communicated under VSA 265.
AUD-025.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 18; VSA 265; VSA 700.
Analysis: True. The FS audit opinion addresses whether the FS are true and fair, not IC. With ineffective controls, the auditor expands substantive work (a substantive approach); with sufficient appropriate evidence, an unmodified opinion is still possible. Significant deficiencies must be communicated in writing to governance and management (VSA 265).

AUD-026.q: Match each test-of-control technique with an example:
p: Checking approval marks on payment requests
Watching the storekeeper check goods on receipt
Asking the chief accountant how exceptions are handled
AUD-026.x:
Basis: VSA 500 paras A14–A25; VSA 330.
Analysis: Inspection – viewing approval marks on payment requests; observation – watching the storekeeper check goods on receipt; re-performance – the auditor redoing the entity's bank reconciliation; inquiry – asking the chief accountant how exceptions are handled.
Note: Re-performance gives the strongest evidence; inquiry is weakest and insufficient alone (AUD-019).

AUD-027.q: A monthly control (12 times/year) is key to a significant risk. Per common practice, the sample size is usually:
AUD-027.e: For monthly controls, 2–5 is typical; higher risk means the upper end.
AUD-027.x:
Basis: Audit practice on sample sizes by control frequency; VSA 530.
Analysis: For a monthly control (12/year), firms' tables usually pick 2–5; a key control over a significant risk should lean to the high end (5).
Distractors: B – one is for annual or automated controls; C – 25–60 is for daily/multiple-daily controls; D – testing all isn't required.
Note: This is practice, not a figure in VSA (ICA-078).

AUD-028.q: When testing management review controls (MRCs), the auditor should assess:
AUD-028.e: A title doesn't prove an effective review.
o: The reviewer's criteria and investigation thresholds
Precision sufficient to detect material misstatement
Evidence of investigating and resolving exceptions
The reviewer's job title is enough
AUD-028.x:
Basis: VSA 330; VSA 500 para 9 (IPE); MRC testing practice.
Analysis: Evaluate: (A) the reviewer's criteria and investigation thresholds; (B) precision sufficient to detect potentially material misstatements; (C) evidence of investigating and resolving exceptions; (D) reliability of the data (IPE) used (ICA-098).
Distractors: (E) A senior title doesn't prove the review was effective (ICA-055).

AUD-029.q: A dual-purpose test checks both control operating effectiveness and transaction details on the same document.
AUD-029.e: True. E.g., inspecting an invoice for approval and checking amount and account.
AUD-029.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para A23.
Analysis: True. A dual-purpose test works on the same document both ways: testing the control (approval, three-way match) and the details (amount, account, period). It saves time but must be designed to meet both tests' objectives (sample size, appropriate population).

AUD-030.q: The auditor tests inventory count controls by:
AUD-030.e: Count attendance tests controls and gives substantive evidence (test counts).
o: Attending the count: observing compliance with instructions, control of count sheets, handling movements
AUD-030.x:
Basis: VSA 501 paras 4–8.
Analysis: Attending the count: evaluate management's instructions and procedures; observe compliance (counting, recording, controlling pre-numbered tags, handling movements and damaged goods); inspect inventory; test-count (records → floor and back). It is both a test of controls and substantive evidence of existence.
Distractors: B – reading minutes afterwards can't verify the process; C – inquiry isn't enough; D – supplier confirmations are irrelevant.

AUD-031.q: The entity uses an external payroll service organisation. The auditor has a SOC 1 Type 2 report for 01/01–30/09. For 01/10–31/12, the auditor needs:
o: A bridge letter and further procedures on control changes; test complementary user controls
A full on-site test at the service organisation
AUD-031.x:
Basis: VSA 402 para 16, A42–A43.
Analysis: The SOC 1 Type 2 covers 1 Jan–30 Sep only → a gap for 1 Oct–31 Dec. The auditor needs: a bridge letter from the service organisation confirming no significant control changes; additional procedures on changes in the remaining period; tests of complementary user entity controls (CUECs) at the entity (e.g., payroll-to-HR reconciliation, approval of pay changes).
Distractors: B ignores three months; C is usually impractical and unnecessary; D – a material item can't be skipped.

AUD-032.q: Tests of controls provide evidence on whether a specific account balance is accurate.
AUD-032.e: False. ToC give evidence on control effectiveness; substantive procedures test for misstatements in balances.
AUD-032.x:
Basis: VSA 330 para 4.
Analysis: False. Tests of controls give evidence on whether controls effectively prevent, detect and correct misstatements – indirectly lowering risk. Substantive procedures (tests of details, substantive analytics) directly detect material misstatements in balances and transactions. Exception: dual-purpose tests (AUD-029).

AUD-033.q: The auditor tests the credit limit control at a distributor. An effective procedure:
AUD-033.e: Combines the automated control and approval of master-data changes.
o: Inspect ERP limit configuration, limit-change logs and approvals; attempt an over-limit order in a test environment
AUD-033.x:
Basis: VSA 330; ICA-067.
Analysis: The credit-limit control has an automated part (ERP blocking over-limit orders) and a manual part (approving limit changes in master data, approving exceptions). Effective procedures: inspect limit configuration in the ERP; review limit change logs and matching approvals (who can edit, was it approved); try creating an over-limit order in a test environment to confirm the block.
Distractors: B – inquiry isn't enough; C and D don't test the control.

AUD-034.q: Match each procedure with the main assertion tested:
AUD-034.e: The direction of testing (ledger → document or vice versa) determines the assertion.
p: Vouch from the sales ledger to delivery documents
Trace from delivery documents to the sales ledger
Search for unrecorded liabilities after year-end
AUD-034.x:
Basis: VSA 500 paras A51–A52 (direction of testing).
Analysis: Sales ledger → shipping documents: recorded revenue is real (occurrence). Shipping documents → sales ledger: all deliveries are recorded (completeness). Searching for unrecorded liabilities after year-end: payables completeness (AUD-035). Testing net realisable value: inventory valuation (VAS 02).
Note: Direction determines the assertion tested – sampling from the ledger can't find omitted items.

AUD-035.q: The most effective procedure to detect unrecorded liabilities is:
AUD-035.e: Confirming large balances mainly tests existence; unrecorded liabilities may show a zero balance.
o: Examine payments and invoices received after period end, matching them to the period the obligation arose
AUD-035.x:
Basis: VSA 500; VSA 505 para A24.
Analysis: Unrecorded liabilities may show a nil ledger balance → sampling from the ledger can't find them. Most effective: examine payments and invoices received after year-end (a source outside the ledger) and see whether the obligation arose before or after the cut-off; if before and unrecorded → omission.
Distractors: B – confirming large balances mainly tests existence; C only views what's recorded; D – inquiry isn't enough.

AUD-036.q: For supplier confirmations, blank confirmations should be used and suppliers with small or zero balances but large annual transactions should be selected.
AUD-036.x:
Basis: VSA 505 paras A6–A7, A24.
Analysis: True. For payables the main risk is understatement (completeness). Blank confirmations make suppliers fill in balances from their own books → more independent evidence. Include suppliers with small/nil balances but large annual activity, because that's where omitted liabilities hide.

AUD-037.q: A customer doesn't reply to a positive receivable confirmation. A suitable alternative procedure:
AUD-037.e: Subsequent receipts are strong evidence of existence.
o: Examine subsequent cash receipts, contracts, delivery documents and invoices
Resend the same letter through the client
AUD-037.x:
Basis: VSA 505 para 12, A18.
Analysis: For a non-response to a positive confirmation, perform alternative procedures: examine subsequent cash receipts (strong evidence of existence and collectability) and match contracts, shipping documents and invoices to the balance.
Distractors: B – silence isn't confirmation; C – sending via the entity loses control of the process (AUD-038); D – dropping the item biases sampling results.

AUD-038.q: Select ALL requirements for controlling the confirmation process:
AUD-038.e: Losing control of confirmations reduces reliability and raises fraud risk.
o: The auditor sends and receives directly
Verify confirming parties' addresses/emails independently of client data
No client interference in the process
Let client accountants collect replies to save time
AUD-038.x:
Basis: VSA 505 para 7, A4–A8.
Analysis: The auditor must control the confirmation process: (A) send and receive directly; (B) verify the confirming party's address/email independently (business registry, website) – not only entity-supplied details, to avoid reaching a colluding party; (C) record and investigate differences; (D) keep the entity out.
Distractors: (E) Letting the entity's accountant receive replies destroys reliability and enables alteration or forgery.

AUD-039.q: At the stock count the auditor test-counts 50 items with book value VND 2,000 million and finds a shortfall of 30 million. What is the error rate on sample value (%)?
AUD-039.e: 30/2,000 = 1.5%; project to the population and investigate the cause.
AUD-039.x:
Basis: VSA 501; VSA 530 para 14.
Working: Error rate on sample value = 30 / 2,000 = 1.5%.
Analysis: Find the cause (loss, recording error, cut-off), project the misstatement to the population (e.g., 1.5% × total inventory) and compare with performance materiality; if systemic, ask the entity to recount the affected area.
Check: 2,000 × 1.5% = 30 ✓.

AUD-040.q: The entity's inventory is held in a third-party warehouse. A suitable procedure:
AUD-040.e: VSA 501 requires evidence on existence and condition of goods held by third parties.
o: Confirm with the custodian and/or attend a count there, assessing the third party's competence and objectivity
Rely only on the entity's stock records
AUD-040.x:
Basis: VSA 501 para 8; VSA 505.
Analysis: Material inventory held by a third party → obtain evidence of existence and condition by confirming quantities and condition with the custodian and/or inspecting or attending a count at the warehouse; assess the third party's competence and objectivity (any link to the entity – collusion risk).
Distractors: B – the entity's records aren't independent; C – the stock is still the entity's asset; D – inquiry isn't enough.

AUD-041.q: Analytical test of depreciation: average machinery cost VND 6,000 million, 8-year life. What is expected depreciation (VND million)?
AUD-041.e: 6,000/8 = 750 million; compare with recorded depreciation to identify differences to explain.
AUD-041.x:
Basis: VSA 520 (substantive analytics – independent expectation).
Working: Expected depreciation = average cost / useful life = 6,000 / 8 = VND 750 million.
Analysis: Compare with recorded depreciation; differences beyond the threshold must be explained (fully depreciated assets still in use, mid-year additions/disposals, changed lives) and corroborated.
Check: 750 × 8 = 6,000 ✓.

AUD-042.q: The key substantive procedure for the risk of capitalising repairs as PP&E:
o: Sample PP&E additions, inspect documents and nature (upgrade extending life vs maintenance)
AUD-042.x:
Basis: VSA 500; VAS 03 para 14 (subsequent expenditure).
Analysis: Improper capitalisation = booking routine repairs into fixed-asset cost → higher assets, lower expenses, higher profit. Key procedure: sample additions (ledger → documents) and examine nature: only upgrades increasing future economic benefits (longer life, more capacity) may be capitalised; maintenance restoring original condition must be expensed.
Distractors: B – a count proves existence, not the nature of spend; C – depreciation is a consequence; D is irrelevant.

AUD-043.q: Select ALL suitable substantive procedures for cash:
AUD-043.e: Bank confirmations also reveal undisclosed obligations and pledged collateral.
o: Bank confirmations of balances, loans, guarantees and pledged assets
Review bank reconciliations and old reconciling items
Test inter-account transfers around period end (kiting)
AUD-043.x:
Basis: VSA 505; VSA 500.
Analysis: Cash procedures: (A) bank confirmations covering balances, loans, guarantees and pledged assets – also revealing undisclosed obligations and collateral; (B) testing bank reconciliations and old reconciling items (unpresented cheques, deposits in transit); (C) a cash count at year-end; (D) testing inter-account transfers around year-end for kiting (receipt recorded but not the outgoing side → inflated cash).
Distractors: (E) Reading the cash book alone gives no independent evidence.

AUD-044.q: Sales cut-off testing selects delivery documents a few days either side of period end and matches them to the revenue period.
AUD-044.e: True, combined with checking returns early next period.
AUD-044.x:
Basis: VSA 500 (cut-off procedures).
Analysis: True. Selecting shipping documents a few days either side of year-end and matching them to the revenue period → catches revenue booked early (shipped next year, recorded this year) or late. Also examine early-next-year returns and allowances – a sign of year-end fictitious sales later reversed.

AUD-045.q: A construction company recognises revenue by stage of completion using actual/total estimated costs. The key procedure:
AUD-045.e: Cost-to-complete estimates are material and easily manipulated to flatter profit.
o: Assess reliability of total cost estimates (compare budgets vs actuals on completed contracts, interview project engineers), test actual costs and cut-off
AUD-045.x:
Basis: VSA 540; VAS 15 (construction contracts – percentage of completion).
Analysis: Cost-to-cost method: % complete = cumulative actual cost / total estimated cost. Cutting the total estimate → higher % complete → more revenue and profit → the estimate is material and easily manipulated. Procedures: assess estimate reliability (compare estimates with outcomes on completed contracts – retrospective review; interview project engineers); test actual costs incurred (real, correct contract) and cut-off.
Distractors: B, C and D don't test the revenue basis.

AUD-046.q: For payroll at a 500-employee service company, an effective substantive analytical procedure:
AUD-046.e: An independent, precise expectation makes analytics persuasive.
o: Expected payroll = monthly average headcount × average pay, adjusted for raises; compare to recorded
Compare totals with last year without further analysis
AUD-046.x:
Basis: VSA 520 para 5, A12–A16.
Analysis: Substantive analytics work when the expectation is independent and precise: expected payroll = average monthly headcount × average pay (by grade/group), adjusted for in-year raises and bonuses; compare with the books and investigate differences beyond the threshold.
Distractors: B – a crude year-on-year total ignores headcount changes and raises; C – one month isn't representative; D – inquiry isn't analytics.

AUD-047.q: Consider these statements on substantive procedures:
AUD-047.e: Counts mainly prove existence; unrecorded liabilities must be sought outside the ledger.
o: Receivable confirmations mainly give evidence of existence, little on valuation.
Count attendance proves ownership of inventory.
Inspecting recorded purchase invoices detects unrecorded liabilities.
AUD-047.x:
Basis: VSA 500; VSA 501; VSA 505.
Analysis: True – receivable confirmations mainly prove existence; acknowledging a debt doesn't mean paying it (little valuation evidence). False – attending a count proves existence and condition; ownership needs invoices and contracts (goods held for others may sit in the warehouse). True – subsequent receipts support collectability. False – recorded invoices can't reveal unrecorded liabilities; use sources outside the ledger (AUD-035).

AUD-048.q: For bank loans, a key 'presentation and disclosure' procedure:
AUD-048.e: A covenant breach can make a loan repayable on demand → current liability.
o: Check current/non-current classification, collateral, rates and covenant compliance; a breach may require current classification
AUD-048.x:
Basis: VSA 500; IAS 1 para 74 (IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 from 2027 but keeps the classification requirement); Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (current/non-current classification).
Analysis: Presentation and disclosure procedures: classify current/non-current by remaining maturity; disclose collateral, rates and terms; test covenant compliance – if breached and the lender can demand immediate repayment with no waiver before period-end, classify as current.
Distractors: B, C and D don't cover presentation and disclosure.

AUD-049.q: The auditor can rely entirely on the entity's count sheets without attending the count when inventory is material.
AUD-049.e: False. VSA 501 requires attendance when inventory is material, unless impracticable with alternative procedures.
AUD-049.x:
Basis: VSA 501 paras 4, 7.
Analysis: False. When inventory is material, the auditor must attend the count (unless impracticable) to evaluate instructions, observe, inspect and test-count. If attendance is impossible, perform alternative procedures; if none are possible → a scope limitation (VSA 705). The entity's count sheets aren't independent evidence.

AUD-050.q: In journal entry testing responding to management override, the auditor should prioritise:
AUD-050.e: These are common characteristics of fraudulent entries.
o: Entries to rarely used accounts, by unusual users, at period end/after close, round sums, without descriptions
AUD-050.x:
Basis: VSA 240 para 32a, A41–A44.
Analysis: Prioritise entries with risk features: posted to unusual or seldom-used accounts; made by people who don't usually post; at period-end or after close; round numbers or consistent endings; no description or support; consolidation adjustments – common traits of fraudulent entries.
Distractors: B – routine automated entries carry little override risk; C – smallest value isn't a risk criterion; D – a random March sample misses period-end risk.

AUD-051.q: Conditions for an effective substantive analytical procedure:
AUD-051.e: The more precise the expectation, the more persuasive the evidence.
o: A predictable relationship, reliable data, a sufficiently precise expectation and a clear acceptable difference threshold
Just comparing this year with last
AUD-051.x:
Basis: VSA 520 para 5, A12–A16.
Analysis: Substantive analytics work when: (1) data relationships are plausible and predictable (e.g., room revenue – occupancy – rate); (2) data used for the expectation is reliable (independent, tested); (3) the expectation is precise enough to detect material misstatement; (4) an acceptable difference threshold is set in advance and larger gaps investigated.
Distractors: B – a bare year-on-year comparison is usually imprecise; C – verbal information is unreliable; D – without a threshold no conclusion is possible.

AUD-052.q: A 200-room hotel, average occupancy 70%, average daily rate VND 1.5 million, 365 days. What is expected room revenue (VND million)?
AUD-052.x:
Basis: VSA 520 (independent expectation).
Working: Expected room revenue = rooms × occupancy × days × average rate = 200 × 70% × 365 × 1.5 = 140 × 365 × 1.5 = 51,100 × 1.5 = VND 76,650 million.
Analysis: Room-nights sold = 51,100. Occupancy and average rate should come from the hotel's PMS after testing its reliability.
Check: 76,650 / 1.5 / 365 = 140 rooms/night = 70% × 200 ✓.

AUD-053.q: A 200-room hotel, 70% average occupancy, average rate VND 1.5 million/night, 365 days → expected room revenue VND 76,650 million. Recorded room revenue is 80,000 million; acceptable difference 2,000 million. By how much does the difference exceed the threshold (VND million)?
AUD-053.e: Difference = 80,000 − 76,650 = 3,350; excess 3,350 − 2,000 = 1,350 million → investigate and obtain further evidence.
AUD-053.x:
Basis: VSA 520 para 7.
Working: Difference = 80,000 − 76,650 = 3,350 million; excess over threshold = 3,350 − 2,000 = VND 1,350 million.
Analysis: Recorded revenue exceeds the expectation beyond the threshold → investigate: ask management and corroborate (event or surcharge revenue mixed into rooms; higher actual rates; cut-off; fictitious revenue). Don't accept explanations without evidence.
Check: 76,650 + 2,000 + 1,350 = 80,000 ✓.

AUD-054.q: Monetary unit sampling (MUS) has which feature?
AUD-054.e: Understated or omitted items have little chance of selection under MUS.
o: Each currency unit has equal selection probability, so larger items are more likely selected; suited to overstatement testing
Best for detecting understatement and zero balances
AUD-054.x:
Basis: VSA 530 appendix 4 (monetary unit sampling).
Analysis: MUS treats each currency unit as a sampling unit → larger items are more likely selected; items ≥ the interval are certain to be. It suits testing overstatement (existence, occurrence).
Distractors: B – understated, omitted or nil-balance items have little or no chance of selection → MUS doesn't suit completeness; C – an interval = population / sample size is required; D – MUS is for substantive tests.

AUD-055.q: MUS: receivables population VND 50,000 million, tolerable misstatement 2,500 million, reliability factor 3 (95%, no expected errors). What is the sample size?
AUD-055.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (MUS – sample size).
Working: n = population value × reliability factor / tolerable misstatement = 50,000 × 3 / 2,500 = 150,000 / 2,500 = 60 items; interval = 50,000 / 60 ≈ VND 833 million.
Analysis: Factor 3 (≈ 3.0 for 95% confidence with no expected misstatement – Poisson). Expected misstatements would increase the sample.
Check: 60 × 833.3 ≈ 50,000 ✓.

AUD-056.q: MUS with a sampling interval of VND 800 million. An item recorded at 200 million is actually 150 million. What projected misstatement arises for its interval (VND million)?
AUD-056.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (MUS – projecting misstatement).
Working: Error = 200 − 150 = 50 million; tainting = 50 / 200 = 25%; projected = 25% × interval 800 = VND 200 million.
Analysis: An item smaller than the interval represents the whole interval → its tainting applies to the full 800 million.
Check: 200 / 800 = 25% ✓.

AUD-057.q: MUS: an item recorded at VND 1,000 million (above the 800 million interval) has a 40 million error. What is the projected misstatement for this item (VND million)?
AUD-057.e: Items ≥ the interval are tested 100%; the error counts at actual, not projected.
AUD-057.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (MUS – large items).
Working: The 1,000 million item ≥ the 800 million interval → tested 100% (certain selection) → projected misstatement = actual = VND 40 million.
Analysis: Large items don't represent the rest of the population, so their tainting isn't projected; only the actual error is added.
Distractors: Applying 4% × 800 = 32 million or other projections is methodologically wrong.

AUD-058.q: The auditor may exclude an 'anomalous' misstatement from projection only with a high degree of certainty that it is not representative of the population.
AUD-058.e: True under VSA 530; additional procedures must support it.
AUD-058.x:
Basis: VSA 530 para 13, A19.
Analysis: True. An anomaly – clearly unrepresentative of the population – may be excluded from projection only when the auditor gains a high degree of certainty, through additional procedures, that it doesn't affect the rest. The actual misstatement is still accumulated (VSA 450).

AUD-059.q: A retailer's gross margin rises from 22% to 28% while the industry declines. The most likely risk:
AUD-059.e: Moves contrary to the industry need independent corroboration.
o: Revenue overstatement or COGS understatement (missed issues, costing errors, cut-off)
AUD-059.x:
Basis: VSA 520; VSA 240.
Analysis: Gross margin rising from 22% to 28% while the industry falls is unusual. Most likely: overstated revenue (fictitious, early) or understated COGS (missed issues, wrong costing, COGS cut-off mismatched with revenue, costs wrongly capitalised into inventory). It must be explained with independent evidence (product mix, prices, supplier rebates).
Distractors: C and D – selling and interest costs sit below gross profit; B is wrong.

AUD-060.q: Select ALL selection methods that are statistical or suitable for projection:
AUD-060.e: Block selection is generally not representative of the whole year.
o: Systematic selection with a random start
Block selection of all December transactions
AUD-060.x:
Basis: VSA 530 appendix 4 (selection methods).
Analysis: Suitable for projection (every item has a chance of selection): (A) random selection; (B) systematic selection with a random start (provided the population has no pattern matching the interval); (C) MUS.
Distractors: (D) Block selection of all December items gives other months no chance → not representative of the year and not projectable (though it may serve cut-off purposes).

AUD-061.q: Using data analytics on 100% of revenue entries, the auditor finds 120 exceptions. The right approach:
AUD-061.e: Analytics identify items; corroborating evidence is still required.
o: Group exceptions, understand causes, test risky groups in detail; exceptions aren't misstatements until tested
AUD-061.x:
Basis: VSA 500; VSA 330.
Analysis: CAATs on 100% of entries identify, they don't prove; 120 exceptions aren't yet errors. Approach: group by features (same cause, preparer, account), understand causes, test the risky groups in detail with support; close groups explained by evidence.
Distractors: B concludes without evidence; C – ignoring exceptions breaches scepticism; D – five random picks don't cover the risky groups.

AUD-062.q: Testing 40 receivables (sample value VND 8,000 million) reveals overstatement of 160 million. The population is 40,000 million. What is the projected misstatement using the ratio method (VND million)?
AUD-062.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (projection – ratio method).
Working: Sample error rate = 160 / 8,000 = 2%; projected = 2% × 40,000 = VND 800 million.
Analysis: Compare the projection (plus other misstatements) with tolerable misstatement; if close or above → extend procedures, ask the entity to investigate and adjust.
Check: 800 / 40,000 = 2% ✓.

AUD-063.q: Analytical procedures are mandatory at the planning and completion stages.
AUD-063.e: True under VSA 315 and VSA 520; they're optional as substantive procedures.
AUD-063.x:
Basis: VSA 315 para 6b; VSA 520 para 6.
Analysis: True. Analytics are mandatory: (1) at planning – as risk assessment procedures (VSA 315); (2) at completion – to form an overall conclusion on whether the FS are consistent with the auditor's understanding (VSA 520 para 6). During fieldwork, substantive analytics are optional – used when suitable and efficient.

AUD-064.q: The sampling risk in substantive testing with more serious consequences for audit effectiveness is:
AUD-064.e: This risk affects effectiveness (wrong opinion); the other mainly affects efficiency.
o: Concluding no material misstatement when one exists (incorrect acceptance)
Concluding a material misstatement exists when it doesn't
AUD-064.x:
Basis: VSA 530 paras A1–A3 (sampling risk).
Analysis: Incorrect acceptance (concluding no material misstatement when there is one) hits audit effectiveness → possibly an inappropriate opinion – the graver consequence. Incorrect rejection (concluding misstatement when there is none) mainly hits efficiency – extra work later shows the initial conclusion wrong.
Distractors: C and D aren't sampling-risk types.

AUD-065.q: A regression of a factory's power costs on output gives R² = 0.92. Implication for substantive analytics:
AUD-065.e: Reliability of input data (output volumes) must still be tested.
o: A strong relationship enabling a precise expectation if output data are reliable
AUD-065.x:
Basis: VSA 520 paras A12–A16.
Analysis: R² = 0.92 → 92% of the variation in power cost is explained by output → a tight relationship; regression can give a precise expectation for substantive analytics. Conditions: reliable output data (independent of accounting, tested) and no structural change (new lines, tariff changes).
Distractors: B – a good expectation doesn't prove no misstatement; it must still be compared with the books; C and D are wrong.

AUD-066.q: The entity defines 'slow-moving' stock as no issues for 12 months. The auditor uses an ERP ageing report. The first step:
AUD-066.e: Evidence based on a wrong report leads to wrong conclusions.
o: Test the report (IPE) for completeness and accuracy: last-issue logic, total agreed to the ledger
AUD-066.x:
Basis: VSA 500 para 9 (information produced by the entity).
Analysis: The ERP ageing report is IPE – evidence based on it is reliable only if the report is complete and accurate. First step: test the 'last issue date' logic (do internal transfers 'refresh' old stock?), report parameters, and reconcile the total to the inventory ledger.
Distractors: B – accepting it outright breaches VSA 500; C and D don't first secure the underlying data.

AUD-067.q: Under VSA 540, approaches to auditing estimates include:
AUD-067.e: Approaches can be combined depending on risk.
o: Testing how management made the estimate; developing an independent point or range; using events up to the report date
AUD-067.x:
Basis: VSA 540 para 13.
Analysis: The auditor uses one or more of: (a) events up to the report date (e.g., subsequent receipts for a bad-debt allowance); (b) testing how management made the estimate and its data and assumptions; (c) testing controls over the estimation process; (d) developing an independent point estimate or range.
Distractors: B accepts without evaluation; C and D are insufficient.
Note: The current VSA 540 is based on ISA 540 before its 2018 revision.

AUD-068.q: Management estimates a warranty provision of VND 500 million; the auditor's reasonable range is 620–700 million. What minimum misstatement is accumulated (VND million)?
AUD-068.e: The estimate is outside the range → misstatement at least 620 − 500 = 120 million VND.
AUD-068.x:
Basis: VSA 540 para A116; VSA 450.
Working: Management's 500 lies outside the reasonable range 620–700 → minimum misstatement = nearest bound − estimate = 620 − 500 = VND 120 million.
Analysis: When an estimate falls outside the range, the misstatement is at least the distance to the nearest bound (a judgemental misstatement). Don't use the midpoint (660) without grounds for a specific point estimate.
Check: 500 + 120 = 620 ✓.

AUD-069.q: Several management estimates all sit at the most profitable end of reasonable ranges. The auditor should:
AUD-069.e: Cumulative bias can cause material misstatement even if each estimate is reasonable.
o: Consider indicators of management bias in aggregate and the impact on fraud risk assessment
Do nothing as each is within range
Adjust all to the low end
AUD-069.x:
Basis: VSA 540 para 21, A124–A125; VSA 240 para 32b.
Analysis: Each estimate is within range, but all sit at the most profit-friendly end → a sign of systematic management bias. Evaluate the aggregate effect (accumulated bias may be material), its impact on fraud risk assessment and reliance on representations, and communicate with governance.
Distractors: B ignores the indicator; C – no basis to move each to the low bound; D overreacts.

AUD-070.q: Select ALL procedures to identify undisclosed related parties:
AUD-070.e: Management's list may be incomplete, especially if concealment is intended.
o: Search business registration data of major counterparties (representatives, addresses, shareholders)
Examine unusual transactions: off-market pricing, no contracts, prepayments
Read bank confirmations for guarantees to third parties
Rely only on management's related-party list
AUD-070.x:
Basis: VSA 550 paras 14–16.
Analysis: Procedures to find undisclosed related parties: (A) business-registry searches on major counterparties – shared representatives, addresses or shareholders with management; (B) reading board and AGM minutes; (C) watching for unusual transactions – off-market prices, no contract, prepayment, favourable terms; (D) bank confirmations of guarantees for third parties.
Distractors: (E) Relying only on management's list – it may be incomplete, especially if concealment is intended.

AUD-071.q: An assertion in the FS that related-party transactions were at arm's length must not stand without sufficient supporting evidence.
AUD-071.e: True. VSA 550 requires evaluating management's assertion.
AUD-071.x:
Basis: VSA 550 para 24.
Analysis: True. If management asserts in the FS that related-party transactions were on arm's-length terms, the auditor must obtain sufficient appropriate evidence for that assertion (market price comparisons, independent valuations). Without it → unsupported → request a disclosure change or consider a modified opinion.
Note: As phrased, the subject is management's assertion within the FS.

AUD-072.q: Which subsequent event is NON-adjusting (disclosed if material)?
AUD-072.e: The fire is a condition arising after period end.
o: A factory fire in January next year
A customer owing at 31/12 goes bankrupt after long-standing difficulties
A court ruling on a lawsuit existing at 31/12
Discovery of fraud misstating this year's FS
AUD-072.x:
Basis: VSA 560; VAS 23 paras 03, 08–09.
Analysis: Non-adjusting events reflect conditions arising after period-end – a factory fire in January (assets were fine at 31 Dec) → disclose only if material.
Distractors: B – a customer's bankruptcy from longstanding difficulties evidences conditions at 31 Dec → adjust the allowance; C – a ruling on an existing lawsuit → adjust the provision; D – fraud discovered that misstates this year's FS → adjust.

AUD-073.q: After the audit report is issued, the auditor learns of a fact that would have changed the report. The auditor should:
AUD-073.e: VSA 560 sets responsibilities for facts discovered after issuance.
o: Discuss with management; if FS are amended, perform necessary procedures and issue a new report; if not, act to prevent reliance on the old report
AUD-073.x:
Basis: VSA 560 paras 14–17.
Analysis: After issue, on learning of a fact that would have changed the report: discuss with management (and governance) whether the FS need amending. If amended: perform necessary procedures, extend subsequent-events review to the new report date, and issue a new report with an explanatory paragraph. If management neither amends nor informs users: act to prevent reliance on the old report (notifications, legal advice).
Distractors: B – responsibility remains; C – the auditor can't amend the FS; D is insufficient.

AUD-074.q: Select ALL indicators casting doubt on going concern:
AUD-074.e: Dividends from profits are a positive sign.
o: Large operating losses and persistently negative operating cash flow
Loss of key customers or suppliers
AUD-074.x:
Basis: VSA 570 para A2.
Analysis: Going-concern indicators: (A) current liabilities exceeding current assets (negative working capital); (B) large operating losses and persistently negative operating cash flow; (C) covenant breaches, inability to roll over or refinance; (D) loss of key customers, suppliers or markets (ICA-096).
Distractors: (E) Regular dividends from profits are positive (arrears or suspension would be the indicator).

AUD-075.q: A material uncertainty over going concern exists and is adequately disclosed. The appropriate opinion:
AUD-075.e: If disclosure is inadequate, the opinion is qualified or adverse.
o: Unmodified with a 'Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern' section
AUD-075.x:
Basis: VSA 570 paras 19–20; VSA 705; VSA 706.
Analysis: A material uncertainty exists, the going-concern basis is still appropriate and the FS disclose it adequately → an unmodified opinion with a paragraph on the material uncertainty related to going concern. Inadequate disclosure → qualified or adverse. Basis inappropriate yet still used → adverse.
Distractors: B, C and D don't fit adequate disclosure (a disclaimer only in rare cases of multiple uncertainties).
Note: The 2012 VSA 570 uses an 'Emphasis of Matter' paragraph; the separate heading in the answer follows ISA 570 (Revised 2015). Check the current updated VSA set.

AUD-076.q: Management's going concern assessment should cover at least 12 months from the reporting date.
AUD-076.e: True under VAS 21/IAS 1: at least 12 months from the reporting date, longer if later events are known.
AUD-076.x:
Basis: VSA 570 para 13; VAS 21 para 16; IAS 1 para 26.
Analysis: True. The going-concern assessment must cover at least 12 months from the period-end; if management's is shorter, the auditor asks for it to be extended. The auditor also asks about known events or conditions beyond that horizon (VSA 570 para 15).
Note: ISA 570 (Revised 2024, effective for periods beginning on or after 15 Dec 2026) shifts this to 12 months from FS approval – not applicable in Vietnam unless VSA is updated.

AUD-077.q: Procedures to identify subsequent events up to the report date include:
AUD-077.e: Procedures must cover up to the date of the auditor's report.
o: Reading minutes and latest interim FS; inquiring of management and lawyers; reviewing early next-year transactions
AUD-077.x:
Basis: VSA 560 paras 6–7.
Analysis: Subsequent-events procedures cover period-end to the report date: understand management's procedures for identifying them; inquire of management and governance (and lawyers on litigation); read post-period minutes; read the latest interim FS and budgets; review early-next-year transactions and records.
Distractors: B and C are insufficient; D is wrong – the procedures are required.

AUD-078.q: The entity faces a major damages lawsuit. The most appropriate evidence on the likely outcome:
AUD-078.e: VSA 501 requires direct communication with lawyers when litigation risk is material.
o: A direct letter from the entity's legal counsel on status and assessment
AUD-078.x:
Basis: VSA 501 paras 9–10.
Analysis: With material litigation risk, the auditor communicates directly with the entity's lawyers (letter prepared by management, sent by the auditor) to confirm case status, likely outcome and estimated loss → the basis for a provision or contingent-liability disclosure (VAS 18). A lawyer's refusal or management blocking contact → scope limitation.
Distractors: B – internal representations aren't independent; C – press reports aren't reliable; D – the engagement letter doesn't show the outcome.

AUD-079.q: The auditor reassesses an ECL model: management uses LGD 30%, but evidence supports 45%. High-risk exposure is VND 4,000 million, PD 20%. What is the difference in allowance (VND million)?
AUD-079.e: ECL = EAD × PD × LGD: management 4,000 × 20% × 30% = 240; auditor 4,000 × 20% × 45% = 360; difference 120 million VND.
AUD-079.x:
Basis: VSA 540; IFRS 9 section 5.5 (expected credit losses).
Working: ECL = EAD × PD × LGD. Management: 4,000 × 20% × 30% = 240 million; auditor: 4,000 × 20% × 45% = 360 million; difference = 360 − 240 = VND 120 million.
Analysis: The allowance is understated by 120 million (a judgemental misstatement) if the 45% LGD evidence is more persuasive (historical recoveries, collateral values). Accumulate it (VSA 450).
Check: 4,000 × 20% × 15% = 120 ✓.
Note: Current VAS doesn't use ECL; the question follows IFRS 9.

AUD-080.q: When using a valuation expert engaged by the entity, the auditor must assess the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and understand their work.
AUD-080.x:
Basis: VSA 500 para 8 (management's expert); VSA 620 (auditor's expert).
Analysis: True. When using work of an expert engaged by the entity as evidence, the auditor must: evaluate competence, capabilities and objectivity (any interests in the entity); understand the work (scope, methods, assumptions); and evaluate its appropriateness as evidence for the relevant assertion.

AUD-081.q: The entity sells property to a company owned by its chairman at 30% below independent valuation. Risk and procedures:
AUD-081.e: Related-party transactions outside the normal course are significant risks.
o: Off-market related-party transaction transferring value; check required approvals, economic substance, disclosure and tax (transfer pricing)
No risk as a contract exists
AUD-081.x:
Basis: VSA 550 para 23; Law on Enterprises 2020 Art. 167 (approval of related-party contracts); Decree 132/2020/ND-CP (related-party transactions).
Analysis: Selling property to the chair's company 30% below an independent valuation → an off-market related-party deal suggesting value transfer – a significant risk. Procedures: check approval under the enterprise law (AGM/board, interested parties abstaining); evaluate the business rationale; check related-party disclosures; tax – authorities may impose arm's-length pricing (Decree 132/2020).
Distractors: B, C and D look only at form.

AUD-082.q: In a first-year audit, evidence about opening balances can be obtained by:
AUD-082.e: VSA 510 sets responsibilities for opening balances.
o: Reviewing the predecessor's working papers, current-year procedures giving evidence on openings (e.g., collection of opening receivables), additional procedures
Relying solely on last year's report
AUD-082.x:
Basis: VSA 510 para 6.
Analysis: In a first-year audit, evidence on opening balances includes: prior closing balances correctly brought forward; opening balances reflecting appropriate policies; and one or more of – reviewing the predecessor's working papers; current-year procedures giving evidence on openings (collection of opening receivables, settlement of opening payables); specific extra procedures (e.g., opening inventory – AUD-097).
Distractors: B and C lack evaluation; D is unnecessary.

AUD-083.q: Consider these statements on auditing estimates:
AUD-083.e: An outcome differing from the estimate isn't necessarily a misstatement if the estimate was reasonable when made.
o: High-uncertainty estimates may be significant risks.
Any difference between an estimate and the later outcome proves a misstatement.
The auditor must evaluate key assumptions.
Retrospective review of prior estimates helps assess the estimation process.
AUD-083.x:
Basis: VSA 540 paras 9, 11, A42–A45.
Analysis: True – high-uncertainty estimates may be significant risks (para 11). False – an outcome differing from the estimate isn't necessarily a misstatement if the estimate was reasonable given information available then. True – the auditor evaluates key assumptions' reasonableness. True – a retrospective review of prior estimates (para 9) gauges the process's reliability and reveals bias.

AUD-084.q: Under VSA 450, misstatements are classified as:
AUD-084.e: Classification helps communication with management and aggregate evaluation.
AUD-084.x:
Basis: VSA 450 para A3.
Analysis: Three types: factual – beyond doubt (e.g., wrong invoice amount); judgemental – differences from management judgements on estimates or policies the auditor finds unreasonable (AUD-068); projected – the auditor's best estimate of population misstatement extrapolated from a sample (AUD-062). The split aids communication with management and the aggregate evaluation.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't VSA 450 categories.

AUD-085.q: Uncorrected misstatements: factual 600, judgemental 400, projected 700 (VND million, all overstating profit). Overall materiality is 2,000 million. What percentage of materiality do they represent (%)?
AUD-085.e: (600 + 400 + 700) / 2,000 = 85% → close to materiality; consider undetected misstatement risk and request adjustments.
AUD-085.x:
Basis: VSA 450 para 11, A13.
Working: Total uncorrected = 600 + 400 + 700 = 1,700 million; ratio = 1,700 / 2,000 = 85% of overall materiality.
Analysis: Not above materiality but close → undetected misstatements on top may push it over (the reason performance materiality is set lower). The auditor should consider extending procedures and ask management to correct.
Check: 2,000 × 85% = 1,700 ✓.

AUD-086.q: Uncorrected misstatements comprise factual 600, judgemental 400 and projected 700 (VND million, all overstating profit) – 85% of overall materiality of 2,000. Management refuses to correct the 600 million factual misstatement. The auditor should:
AUD-086.e: Materiality must not be revised just to avoid a modified opinion; small items can be qualitatively material.
o: Understand reasons, evaluate aggregate effect (quantitative and qualitative), communicate with those charged with governance, obtain written representations; consider the appropriate opinion
AUD-086.x:
Basis: VSA 450 paras 8–9, 11–14; VSA 580 para 14; VSA 320 para 12.
Analysis: Management refuses to correct a 600 million factual misstatement: understand why; evaluate aggregate effect quantitatively (85% of materiality) and qualitatively (AUD-087); reassess materiality on actual results only if justified, not to avoid modification; communicate with governance; obtain written representations on uncorrected misstatements; consider the appropriate opinion.
Distractors: B – the auditor doesn't amend the FS; C ignores proximity to materiality and qualitative factors; D – raising materiality to dodge a modified opinion breaches the standards.

AUD-087.q: Select ALL cases where a small misstatement may be qualitatively material:
AUD-087.e: Misclassifications affecting no key metric are usually not qualitatively material.
o: It turns a loss into a profit
It just meets a covenant or bonus target
It changes the reported earnings trend
A misclassification between two expenses affecting no key metric
AUD-087.x:
Basis: VSA 450 para A16; VSA 320 para A1.
Analysis: Small misstatements can be qualitatively material when they: (A) turn a loss into a profit; (B) help meet covenants or bonus targets (AUD-009); (C) stem from management fraud – affecting integrity assessments; (D) mask a change in reported earnings trends or market expectations.
Distractors: (E) A misclassification between two expense lines that affects no key metric is usually not qualitatively material.

AUD-088.q: Match each situation with the opinion type:
AUD-088.e: Distinguishing 'material' from 'pervasive' is key to choosing a modified opinion.
p: Unable to obtain evidence, material and pervasive effect
FS fairly presented in all material respects
AUD-088.x:
Basis: VSA 700; VSA 705 paras 7–10.
Analysis: Two factors decide: nature (material misstatement or inability to obtain evidence) and pervasiveness. Material, not pervasive → qualified; material and pervasive → adverse; unable to obtain evidence, possibly material and pervasive → disclaimer; true and fair in all material respects → unmodified.
Note: A material but non-pervasive scope limitation → qualified.

AUD-089.q: Key audit matters (KAM) under VSA 701 are:
AUD-089.e: KAM don't replace modified opinions or entity disclosures.
o: Matters of most significance in the auditor's judgement, selected from those communicated with governance; required for listed entities
A substitute for a qualified opinion
A list of all misstatements found
AUD-089.x:
Basis: ISA 701 (per the question's stated basis 'VSA 701').
Analysis: KAMs are the matters of most significance in the auditor's judgement for the current audit, selected from those communicated with governance (higher-risk areas, significant judgements, significant events). Required for listed entities' FS.
Distractors: B – they don't replace a modified opinion; C – not a list of misstatements; D – KAMs aren't presented with a disclaimer.
Note: The 2012 VSA set (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC) has no VSA 701; content follows ISA 701. Check the current updated VSA texts for effectiveness.

AUD-090.q: Select ALL items typically in management's written representations (VSA 580):
AUD-090.e: Responsibility for the FS stays with management, not the auditor.
o: All related parties and transactions disclosed
AUD-090.x:
Basis: VSA 580 paras 10–14.
Analysis: Representations cover: (A) responsibility for true and fair FS under the framework; (B) all information, documents and access provided; (C) all transactions recorded; (D) related parties and their transactions fully disclosed (VSA 550); (E) uncorrected misstatements immaterial, with a list attached (VSA 450).
Distractors: (F) Responsibility for the FS stays with management, never shifting to the auditor.

AUD-091.q: Management's written representations can replace other evidence the auditor could reasonably expect to obtain.
AUD-091.e: False. Representations are necessary but not sufficient on their own.
AUD-091.x:
Basis: VSA 580 para 4.
Analysis: False. Written representations are necessary evidence but don't by themselves provide sufficient appropriate evidence on the matters covered, and don't replace other evidence the auditor expects to obtain (e.g., confirmations, counts). Representations inconsistent with other evidence must be investigated.

AUD-092.q: Management refuses to sign the representation on completeness of information. The auditor should:
AUD-092.e: VSA 580 treats this as a severe scope limitation.
o: Reassess management integrity and reliability of other representations; usually leads to a disclaimer
AUD-092.x:
Basis: VSA 580 paras 19–20; VSA 705.
Analysis: Refusing to represent on FS responsibility and completeness of information → reassess management's integrity and the reliability of all representations and other evidence. VSA 580 para 20 requires a disclaimer when these required representations aren't provided (a severe, pervasive scope limitation).
Distractors: B can't be ignored; C – the auditor can't sign for them; D contradicts the standard.

AUD-093.e: Representations are dated as near as practicable to, but not after, the report date.
o: Review subsequent events and going concern
Engagement quality review of the file
Sign and issue the auditor's report
AUD-093.x:
Basis: VSA 450; VSA 520; VSA 560; VSA 570; VSA 580 para 14; VSA 220 paras 19–21.
Analysis: Order: (1) accumulate and evaluate misstatements; (2) final overall analytics (VSA 520 para 6); (3) review subsequent events and going concern; (4) obtain the representation letter; (5) quality review of the file (EQR – AUD-098); (6) sign and issue the report.
Note: The representation letter is dated as near as practicable to, but not after, the report date.

AUD-094.q: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph is used to:
AUD-094.e: An emphasis of matter does not modify the opinion.
o: Draw attention to a matter properly presented/disclosed in the FS that is fundamental to understanding
AUD-094.x:
Basis: VSA 706 paras 6–7.
Analysis: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph draws attention to a matter properly presented or disclosed in the FS that, in the auditor's judgement, is fundamental to users' understanding (e.g., a major disaster affecting operations, unresolved litigation). It doesn't change the opinion.
Distractors: B – a material misstatement needs a modified opinion; C – lack of evidence is a scope limitation; D – it doesn't replace the entity's disclosures.

AUD-095.q: The auditor must read other information (e.g., the annual report) to identify material inconsistencies with the audited FS.
AUD-095.x:
Basis: VSA 720 paras 6–9.
Analysis: True. The auditor must read other information in documents containing the audited FS and report (e.g., the annual report) to identify material inconsistencies with the FS. If found → determine whether the FS or the other information needs revising; if the entity refuses, consider the effect on the report.
Note: VSA 720 (2012) follows the old ISA 720; ISA 720 (Revised 2015) broadens duties and requires an 'Other Information' section in the report.

AUD-096.q: Final analytics: revenue +25%, receivables +80%. Revenue was VND 400 and 500 billion; closing receivables 49.3 and 88.8 billion. What are this year's days sales outstanding (closing AR/revenue × 365, rounded)?
AUD-096.e: 88.8/500 × 365 ≈ 64.8 ≈ 65 days (last year 49.3/400 × 365 ≈ 45). A sharp rise → risk of fictitious or uncollectible revenue.
AUD-096.x:
Basis: VSA 520 para 6 (final analytical procedures).
Working: DSO this year = 88.8 / 500 × 365 = 0.1776 × 365 ≈ 64.8 ≈ 65 days; prior year = 49.3 / 400 × 365 ≈ 45.0 days.
Analysis: Receivables up 80% (88.8/49.3 ≈ 1.80) versus revenue up 25% → DSO from 45 to 65 days → risk of fictitious or early year-end revenue, looser credit, or uncollectible debts not provided for. Extend confirmations, cut-off testing and subsequent-receipts work.
Check: 500 / 400 = 1.25 ✓.

AUD-097.q: In a first-year audit, the auditor couldn't observe opening inventory and has no alternatives; inventory is material but not pervasive. The appropriate opinion:
AUD-097.e: Opening inventory affects this year's COGS; the opinion may be qualified on results and cash flows while the balance sheet is unqualified.
o: Qualified for scope limitation on results and cash flows (effect of opening balances)
AUD-097.x:
Basis: VSA 510 para 10; VSA 705 para A8.
Analysis: Opening inventory feeds this year's COGS (COGS = opening + purchases − closing) → no evidence on it limits scope over results and cash flows; closing inventory was tested, so the balance sheet can stand. Material but not pervasive → a qualified opinion on results and cash flows (unmodified on financial position where law permits).
Distractors: B – adverse is for misstatements, not scope limits; C lacks evidence; D – a disclaimer only if pervasive.

AUD-098.q: An engagement quality review (EQR) is performed:
AUD-098.e: Mandatory for public interest entities and engagements per firm policy.
o: Before the report is issued, by someone not on the engagement, evaluating significant judgements and conclusions
AUD-098.x:
Basis: VSA 220 paras 19–21; VSQC 1 (quality control standard – being replaced by ISQM 1 and ISQM 2 under IAASB).
Analysis: An engagement quality review objectively evaluates the team's significant judgements and conclusions before the report is issued, by a competent person not on the engagement. Required for listed/public-interest entity audits and other engagements per firm policy.
Distractors: B – it must precede issue; C – the engagement partner can't review objectively; D – it doesn't depend on client request.

AUD-099.q: Select ALL matters the auditor must communicate with those charged with governance (VSA 260):
AUD-099.e: Team salaries are not a communication matter.
o: Significant findings: policies, difficulties, uncorrected misstatements
AUD-099.x:
Basis: VSA 260 paras 14–17.
Analysis: The auditor must communicate to governance: (A) the auditor's responsibilities for the FS audit; (B) planned scope and timing (significant risks); (C) significant findings – views on policies, estimates and disclosures, difficulties encountered, uncorrected misstatements, other significant matters; (D) independence – for listed entities, a compliance statement and relationships that may bear on it.
Distractors: (E) Team members' salaries aren't a communication item.

AUD-100.q: At completion the auditor finds evidence of fraud by the CFO. The auditor should:
AUD-100.e: Management fraud is always qualitatively material.
o: Reassess risks and reliability of representations, extend procedures, communicate promptly with higher management and governance; consider legal reporting duties and continuing the engagement
AUD-100.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 35–38, 40–42; VSA 250.
Analysis: Fraud by the CFO – senior management – is always qualitatively material. The auditor: reassesses fraud risk and the reliability of representations and evidence (any collusion?); extends procedures; communicates promptly with management above the CFO and with governance; considers legal reporting duties to authorities (overriding confidentiality); and considers continuing or withdrawing.
Distractors: B talks only to the perpetrator; C – amount doesn't matter; D breaches confidentiality.
